claim: The majority of mitochondrial proteins use N-terminal presequences for targeting to mitochondria.
source: The majority of mitochondrial proteins use N-terminal presequences for targeting to mitochondria and are translocated by the presequence translocase.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of mitochondrial biology, supported by the general scientific knowledge and the context of the manuscript.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins with N-terminal presequences are translocated by the presequence translocase.
source: The majority of mitochondrial proteins use N-terminal presequences for targeting to mitochondria and are translocated by the presequence translocase.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial protein import pathways.

claim: During translocation, proteins threaded through the channel in the inner membrane are handed over to the import motor at the matrix face.
source: During translocation, proteins, threaded through the channel in the inner membrane, are handed over to the import motor at the matrix face.
evidence: This describes the general mechanism of protein translocation, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tim17 is an essential, membrane-embedded subunit of the translocase.
source: Tim17 is an essential, membrane-embedded subunit of the translocase; however, its function is only poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by prior knowledge in the field and is a foundational statement for the study.

claim: The function of Tim17 is only poorly understood.
source: Tim17 is an essential, membrane-embedded subunit of the translocase; however, its function is only poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study and provides justification for the research.

claim: Mutations in TM1 and TM2 of Tim17 impaired the interaction with Tim23.
source: Mutations in TM1 and TM2 impaired the interaction of Tim17 with Tim23, component of the translocation channel, whereas mutations in TM3 compromised binding of the import motor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the BN-PAGE and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutations in TM3 of Tim17 compromised binding of the import motor.
source: Mutations in TM1 and TM2 impaired the interaction of Tim17 with Tim23, component of the translocation channel, whereas mutations in TM3 compromised binding of the import motor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D demonstrating impaired Tim44 binding in TM3 mutants.

claim: Residues in the matrix-facing region of Tim17 are involved in binding of the import motor.
source: We identified residues in the matrix-facing region of Tim17 involved in binding of the import motor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies and crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Different regions of Tim17 have functionally distinct roles.
source: Our results reveal functionally distinct roles of different regions of Tim17 and suggest how they may be involved in handing over the proteins, during their translocation into mitochondria, from the channel to the import motor of the presequence translocase.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing differential effects of mutations in different TM segments.

claim: More than half of mitochondrial proteins carry N-terminal presequences and use the TOM and TIM23 complexes for translocation.
source: More than half of them carry N-terminal presequences and use the TOM and the TIM23 complexes for their translocation across the outer and inner membranes, respectively (Bohnert et al., 2015; Endo et al., 2011; Marom et al., 2011a; Schulz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: IMS-exposed domains of Tim50 and Tim23 serve as receptors of the TIM23 complex.
source: Intermembrane space (IMS)-exposed domains of Tim50 and Tim23 serve as receptors of the TIM23 complex that recognize proteins as soon as they appear at the outlet of the TOM complex (Marom et al., 2011b; Mokranjac et al., 2009; Schulz et al., 2011; Tamura et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tim50 and Tim23 recognize proteins as soon as they appear at the outlet of the TOM complex.
source: Intermembrane space (IMS)-exposed domains of Tim50 and Tim23 serve as receptors of the TIM23 complex that recognize proteins as soon as they appear at the outlet of the TOM complex (Marom et al., 2011b; Mokranjac et al., 2009; Schulz et al., 2011; Tamura et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Proteins are transferred to the translocation channel in the inner membrane in a membrane potential-dependent step.
source: In a membrane potential-dependent step, proteins are then transferred to the translocation channel in the inner membrane formed by membrane-embedded segments of Tim23 and possibly also Tim17 and/or Mgr2 (Alder et al., 2008a; Dekker et al., 1997; Ieva et al., 2014; Martinez-Caballero et al., 2007; Truscott et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The translocation channel in the inner membrane is formed by membrane-embedded segments of Tim23 and possibly also Tim17 and/or Mgr2.
source: In a membrane potential-dependent step, proteins are then transferred to the translocation channel in the inner membrane formed by membrane-embedded segments of Tim23 and possibly also Tim17 and/or Mgr2 (Alder et al., 2008a; Dekker et al., 1997; Ieva et al., 2014; Martinez-Caballero et al., 2007; Truscott et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reflects current understanding with some uncertainty (indicated by 'possibly').

claim: Complete translocation into the matrix is mediated by the import motor of the TIM23 complex.
source: Complete translocation into the matrix is mediated by the import motor of the TIM23 complex, also referred to as PAM (presequence translocase-associated motor).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of mitochondrial protein import.

claim: mtHsp70 is the central component of the import motor.
source: mtHsp70 is the central component of the import motor.
evidence: This is well-established knowledge in the field.

claim: mtHsp70's ATP-dependent action drives translocation of proteins across the inner membrane.
source: Its ATP-dependent action, regulated by the J and J-like proteins Tim14/Pam18 and Tim16/Pam16 and the nucleotide exchange factor Mge1, drives translocation of proteins across the inner membrane (D'Silva et al., 2003; Frazier et al., 2004; Kang et al., 1990; Liu et a., 2003; Mokranjac et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: mtHsp70's action is regulated by Tim14/Pam18, Tim16/Pam16, and Mge1.
source: Its ATP-dependent action, regulated by the J and J-like proteins Tim14/Pam18 and Tim16/Pam16 and the nucleotide exchange factor Mge1, drives translocation of proteins across the inner membrane (D'Silva et al., 2003; Frazier et al., 2004; Kang et al., 1990; Liu et a., 2003; Mokranjac et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tim44 is a peripheral membrane protein that acts as an anchor to recruit the import motor to the translocation channel.
source: Tim44 is a peripheral membrane protein that acts as an anchor to recruit the import motor to the translocation channel (D'Silva et al., 2004; Kozany et al., 2004; Schulz and Rehling, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tim44's N-terminal domain binds to the components of the import motor.
source: Through its N-terminal domain, Tim44 binds to the components of the import motor, whereas its C-terminal domain binds to Tim17 (Banerjee et al., 2015; Schiller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tim44's C-terminal domain binds to Tim17.
source: Through its N-terminal domain, Tim44 binds to the components of the import motor, whereas its C-terminal domain binds to Tim17 (Banerjee et al., 2015; Schiller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tim17 and Tim23 form the core of the TIM23 complex onto which all other subunits assemble.
source: Tim17 and Tim23 form the core of the complex onto which all other subunits assemble (Dekker et al., 1997; Kozany et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both Tim17 and Tim23 are predicted to span the inner membrane with four transmembrane helices.
source: Both proteins are predicted to span the inner membrane with four transmembrane (TM) helices.
evidence: This is based on structural predictions and established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: The TMs of Tim17 and Tim23 share limited sequence similarity.
source: The TMs of Tim17 and Tim23 share limited sequence similarity; however, the two proteins cannot substitute for each other (Ryan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Tim17 and Tim23 cannot substitute for each other.
source: The TMs of Tim17 and Tim23 share limited sequence similarity; however, the two proteins cannot substitute for each other (Ryan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The first two TMs of Tim23 constitute at least part of the translocation channel of the TIM23 complex.
source: The first two TMs of Tim23 constitute at least part of the translocation channel of the TIM23 complex, and they actively respond to changes in the membrane potential across inner membrane (Alder et al., 2008a; Alder et al., 2008b; Malhotra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The first two TMs of Tim23 actively respond to changes in the membrane potential across the inner membrane.
source: The first two TMs of Tim23 constitute at least part of the translocation channel of the TIM23 complex, and they actively respond to changes in the membrane potential across inner membrane (Alder et al., 2008a; Alder et al., 2008b; Malhotra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutations of the first two TMs of Tim23 impair the interaction of Tim23 with Tim17.
source: Mutations of the same segments impair the interaction of Tim23 with Tim17 and thus destabilize the entire TIM23 complex (Demishtein-Zohary et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mutations of the first two TMs of Tim23 destabilize the entire TIM23 complex.
source: Mutations of the same segments impair the interaction of Tim23 with Tim17 and thus destabilize the entire TIM23 complex (Demishtein-Zohary et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a logical consequence of impaired Tim23-Tim17 interaction.

claim: TM3 and TM4 of Tim23 appear to have a stabilizing role in the complex.
source: TM3 and TM4 of Tim23 appear to have a stabilizing role in the complex as their deletion is not lethal (Pareek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited observation that deletion is not lethal.

claim: Deletion of TM3 and TM4 of Tim23 is not lethal.
source: TM3 and TM4 of Tim23 appear to have a stabilizing role in the complex as their deletion is not lethal (Pareek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Essentially nothing is known about the TMs of Tim17.
source: In contrast, essentially nothing is known about the TMs of Tim17.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study and provides justification for the research.

claim: Tim17 contains several GxxxG motifs throughout its four predicted TMs.
source: A schematic presentation of Tim17 topology shows that this protein contains several GxxxG motifs throughout its four predicted TMs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GxxxG motif and its more general variant with consensus sequence (small)xxx(small) are frequently functionally important.
source: GxxxG motif and its more general variant with a consensus sequence (small)xxx(small) are frequently functionally important as they are often involved in interactions between TMs of membrane proteins (Teese and Langosch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: GxxxG motifs are often involved in interactions between TMs of membrane proteins.
source: GxxxG motif and its more general variant with a consensus sequence (small)xxx(small) are frequently functionally important as they are often involved in interactions between TMs of membrane proteins (Teese and Langosch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All residues of the GxxxG motifs in Tim17 are highly evolutionarily conserved.
source: Sequence alignment of Tim17 proteins from a number of species demonstrates that all residues of the motifs are highly evolutionary conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All the glycine, alanine and serine residues of the GxxxG motifs cluster on the same sides of the putative helices.
source: Helical wheel projections of individual TMs show that all the glycine, alanine and serine residues of the motifs cluster on the same sides of the putative helices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on helical wheel projection analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All GxxxG motif mutants of Tim17 were viable.
source: Viable colonies were obtained with all mutants (Figure 1B), suggesting that a certain flexibility in packing of transmembrane segments of Tim17 can be tolerated by yeast cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A certain flexibility in packing of transmembrane segments of Tim17 can be tolerated by yeast cells.
source: Viable colonies were obtained with all mutants (Figure 1B), suggesting that a certain flexibility in packing of transmembrane segments of Tim17 can be tolerated by yeast cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that all mutants were viable.

claim: Six GxxxG motif mutants grew visibly slower than wt cells at 37°C.
source: At 37°C, six mutants grew visibly slower as compared to wt cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Slower growth of GxxxG motif mutants was observed irrespective of whether cells were grown on fermentable or non-fermentable carbon source.
source: Slower growth was observed irrespective of whether the cells were grown on fermentable (glucose, YPD) or non-fermentable carbon source (glycerol, YPG).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from growth assays.

claim: The six temperature-sensitive mutations map to TMs 1 to 3: G25L and G29L in TM1, G62L and G66L in TM2 and G95L and G99L in TM3.
source: The six temperature-sensitive (ts) mutations map to TMs 1 to 3: G25L and G29L in TM1, G62L and G66L in TM2 and G95L and G99L in TM3.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and structural predictions.

claim: G99L mutant grew more slowly than wt even at 30°C.
source: G99L grew more slowly than wt even at 30°C.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation from growth assays.

claim: When protein import into mitochondria is impaired, the precursor form of matrix-localized Hsp60 accumulates in the cytosol.
source: When protein import into mitochondria is impaired, the precursor form of matrix-localized Hsp60 accumulates in the cytosol (Gambill et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All ts mutants showed accumulation of Hsp60 precursor.
source: Analysis of total cell extracts showed accumulation of Hsp60 precursor in all ts mutants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The amount of accumulated Hsp60 precursor correlated with the severity of the growth phenotype.
source: The amount of accumulated precursor correlated with the severity of the growth phenotype.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In G99L mutant, the mature form of Hsp60 was hardly detected.
source: In G99L mutant, the mature form of Hsp60 was hardly detected.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation from immunoblotting.

claim: Impaired import via the TIM23 pathway was observed when radiolabeled precursor proteins were imported into isolated mitochondria.
source: Impaired import via the TIM23 pathway was also observed when radiolabeled precursor proteins were imported into isolated mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduction of import efficiency correlated with the severity of the growth phenotype.
source: The reduction of import efficiency correlated with the severity of the growth phenotype also in these experiments.
evidence: This is based on analysis of import assay data.

claim: The defects were observed irrespective of whether matrix translocation or lateral insertion via the TIM23 pathway was analyzed.
source: The defects were observed irrespective of whether matrix translocation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C) or lateral insertion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–I) via the TIM23 pathway was analyzed, although reduction of matrix translocation was typically more pronounced.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from import assays.

claim: Reduction of matrix translocation was typically more pronounced than reduction of lateral insertion.
source: The defects were observed irrespective of whether matrix translocation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C) or lateral insertion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–I) via the TIM23 pathway was analyzed, although reduction of matrix translocation was typically more pronounced.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data.

claim: Import of ATP/ADP carrier occurred with essentially the same efficiency in all types of mitochondria.
source: Importantly, import of a TIM23-independent protein, ATP/ADP carrier (AAC), occurred with essentially the same efficiency in all types of mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–L), demonstrating that the mutations specifically affected import via the TIM23 pathway.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–L.

claim: The mutations specifically affected import via the TIM23 pathway.
source: Importantly, import of a TIM23-independent protein, ATP/ADP carrier (AAC), occurred with essentially the same efficiency in all types of mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–L), demonstrating that the mutations specifically affected import via the TIM23 pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TIM23-independent import was unaffected.

claim: In wt mitochondria, a dominant ca. 90 kDa complex, consisting of Tim17 and Tim23, was observed.
source: In wt mitochondria, as expected, a dominant ca. 90 kDa complex, consisting of Tim17 and Tim23, was observed (Figure 2C) (Chacinska et al., 2005; Dekker et al., 1997; Popov-Celeketić et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C and supported by citations.

claim: The levels of the 90 kDa complex and of the higher molecular weight species were drastically reduced in all ts mutants of TMs 1 and 2.
source: In contrast, the levels of the 90 kDa complex and of the higher molecular weight species were drastically reduced in all ts mutants of TMs 1 and 2.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from BN-PAGE analysis.

claim: The levels of Tim17 and several other essential TIM23 subunits are indistinguishable among different mitochondria.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of the same samples (Figure 2C, lower panel) shows that the levels of Tim17 and several other essential TIM23 subunits are indistinguishable among different mitochondria, demonstrating that the absence of Tim17-containing complexes is not due to instability of the protein but rather due to the involvement of TMs 1 and 2 of Tim17, directly or indirectly, in the interaction with Tim23.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The absence of Tim17-containing complexes is not due to instability of the protein.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of the same samples (Figure 2C, lower panel) shows that the levels of Tim17 and several other essential TIM23 subunits are indistinguishable among different mitochondria, demonstrating that the absence of Tim17-containing complexes is not due to instability of the protein but rather due to the involvement of TMs 1 and 2 of Tim17, directly or indirectly, in the interaction with Tim23.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that protein levels are unchanged.

claim: TMs 1 and 2 of Tim17 are involved, directly or indirectly, in the interaction with Tim23.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of the same samples (Figure 2C, lower panel) shows that the levels of Tim17 and several other essential TIM23 subunits are indistinguishable among different mitochondria, demonstrating that the absence of Tim17-containing complexes is not due to instability of the protein but rather due to the involvement of TMs 1 and 2 of Tim17, directly or indirectly, in the interaction with Tim23.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced complex formation.

claim: TMs 1 and 2 of Tim23 are important for the interaction with Tim17.
source: This resembles the previous finding that TMs 1 and 2 of Tim23 are important for the interaction with Tim17 (Alder et al., 2008b; Demishtein-Zohary et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The 90 kDa complex was present at essentially wt levels in both TM3 ts mutants.
source: Intriguingly, the 90 kDa complex was present at essentially wt levels in both TM3 ts mutants, suggesting that TM3 has only a minor role in the stability of the 90 kDa Tim17-Tim23 core complex.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from BN-PAGE analysis.

claim: TM3 has only a minor role in the stability of the 90 kDa Tim17-Tim23 core complex.
source: Intriguingly, the 90 kDa complex was present at essentially wt levels in both TM3 ts mutants, suggesting that TM3 has only a minor role in the stability of the 90 kDa Tim17-Tim23 core complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TM3 mutants maintain normal complex levels.

claim: His-tagged but otherwise wt Tim17 efficiently bound to Ni-agarose beads, bringing down Tim23, Tim50 and Tim44.
source: His-tagged but otherwise wt Tim17 efficiently bound to the Ni-agarose beads, bringing down Tim23, Tim50 and Tim44 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Similar amounts of Tim23 were bound to the Ni-agarose beads when the two TM3 mutant mitochondria were analyzed.
source: Similar amounts of Tim23 were bound to the Ni-agarose beads when the two TM3 mutant mitochondria were analyzed, confirming the results obtained by BN-PAGE described above.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from pull-down assays.

claim: Binding of Tim50 was indistinguishable among the three types of mitochondria.
source: Binding of Tim50 was also indistinguishable among the three types of mitochondria, in agreement with the notion that Tim50 is recruited to the complex mainly through its interaction with the IMS-exposed domain of Tim23 (Geissler et al., 2002; Gevorkyan-Airapetov et al., 2009; Yamamoto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from pull-down assays and supported by citations.

claim: Tim50 is recruited to the complex mainly through its interaction with the IMS-exposed domain of Tim23.
source: Binding of Tim50 was also indistinguishable among the three types of mitochondria, in agreement with the notion that Tim50 is recruited to the complex mainly through its interaction with the IMS-exposed domain of Tim23 (Geissler et al., 2002; Gevorkyan-Airapetov et al., 2009; Yamamoto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Binding of Tim44 to the beads was impaired in both TM3 mutants.
source: In contrast, binding of Tim44 to the beads was impaired in both mutants.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from pull-down assays.

claim: In the G99L mutant, essentially no Tim44 was found in the bound fraction.
source: In the G99L mutant, essentially no Tim44 was found in the bound fraction.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from pull-down assays.

claim: During translocation of proteins into mitochondria Tim44 may reach deep into the membrane.
source: Although it is likely that during translocation of proteins into mitochondria Tim44 may reach deep into the membrane (Kanamori et al., 1997), it is generally accepted that the major part of Tim44 is exposed to the matrix, suggesting that its binding site should be found in more matrix-facing regions of Tim17.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a speculative statement ('it is likely').

claim: The major part of Tim44 is exposed to the matrix.
source: Although it is likely that during translocation of proteins into mitochondria Tim44 may reach deep into the membrane (Kanamori et al., 1997), it is generally accepted that the major part of Tim44 is exposed to the matrix, suggesting that its binding site should be found in more matrix-facing regions of Tim17.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tim44's binding site should be found in more matrix-facing regions of Tim17.
source: Although it is likely that during translocation of proteins into mitochondria Tim44 may reach deep into the membrane (Kanamori et al., 1997), it is generally accepted that the major part of Tim44 is exposed to the matrix, suggesting that its binding site should be found in more matrix-facing regions of Tim17.
evidence: This is an inference based on the topology of Tim44.

claim: A binding site of Tim44 has not been found in the matrix-exposed loop between TMs 1 and 2 of Tim17.
source: A binding site of Tim44 has not been found in the matrix-exposed loop between TMs 1 and 2 of Tim17 (Ting et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The mutant of the first half of the loop (residues 104-108) resulted in a lethal phenotype.
source: The mutant of the first half of the loop resulted in a lethal phenotype, whereas the second mutant was viable (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The mutant of the second half of the loop (residues 109-113) was viable.
source: The mutant of the first half of the loop resulted in a lethal phenotype, whereas the second mutant was viable (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The residues potentially involved in Tim44 binding are found in the region 104–108.
source: This result suggests that the residues potentially involved in Tim44 binding are found in the region 104–108.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: There is a highly conserved arginine residue at position 105 of Tim17.
source: Close inspection of this region revealed a highly conserved arginine residue at position 105 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data.

claim: The R105A mutant was viable but displayed a severely reduced and temperature-sensitive growth.
source: The R105A mutant was viable but displayed a severely reduced and temperature-sensitive growth even on fermentable carbon source and was barely viable on non-fermentable carbon source (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from growth assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The R105A mutant was barely viable on non-fermentable carbon source.
source: The R105A mutant was viable but displayed a severely reduced and temperature-sensitive growth even on fermentable carbon source and was barely viable on non-fermentable carbon source (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from growth assays.

claim: Submitochondrial localization of the Tim17R105A mutant was indistinguishable from wt.
source: Submitochondrial localization of the Tim17R105A mutant was indistinguishable from wt (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that impaired biogenesis and an altered topology of Tim17 were not the reasons behind the severe growth phenotype.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Impaired biogenesis and an altered topology of Tim17 were not the reasons behind the severe growth phenotype of R105A.
source: Submitochondrial localization of the Tim17R105A mutant was indistinguishable from wt (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that impaired biogenesis and an altered topology of Tim17 were not the reasons behind the severe growth phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normal localization of the mutant protein.

claim: Impaired growth of R105A was likely due to the impaired protein import via the TIM23 pathway.
source: Impaired growth was likely due to the impaired protein import via the TIM23 pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on import assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Precursor proteins translocated into the matrix or laterally inserted into the inner membrane by the TIM23 complex were imported with reduced efficiencies into mitochondria isolated from tim17R105A cells.
source: Precursor proteins translocated into the matrix or laterally inserted into the inner membrane by the TIM23 complex were imported with reduced efficiencies into mitochondria isolated from tim17R105A cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from import assays.

claim: Import of a TIM23-independent substrate occurred with an efficiency indistinguishable from wt in tim17R105A mitochondria.
source: Import of a TIM23-independent substrate occurred with an efficiency indistinguishable from wt.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from import assays.

claim: A mutant in which arginine 105 was exchanged to lysine showed a very similar growth phenotype to R105A.
source: A mutant in which arginine was exchanged to lysine, thus keeping a positive charge at this position, showed a very similar growth phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that, intriguingly, the charge itself is not sufficient for function.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The charge itself at position 105 is not sufficient for function.
source: A mutant in which arginine was exchanged to lysine, thus keeping a positive charge at this position, showed a very similar growth phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that, intriguingly, the charge itself is not sufficient for function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that R105K has a similar phenotype to R105A.

claim: In wt, Tim44 was immunoprecipitated with antibodies to Tim17, Tim23 and Tim16.
source: In wt, Tim44 was immunoprecipitated with antibodies to Tim17, Tim23 and Tim16, as described previously (Kozany et al., 2004; Popov-Celeketić et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation and supported by citations.

claim: In the R105A mutant, the interaction of Tim44 with the TIM23 complex was severely compromised.
source: In contrast, in the R105A mutant, the interaction of Tim44 with the TIM23 complex was severely compromised (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The interaction between Tim17 and Tim23 in the R105A mutant was indistinguishable from that in wt.
source: However, the interaction between Tim17 and Tim23 in the R105A mutant was indistinguishable from that in wt, in agreement with the results of the analysis of GxxxG motifs described above.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: Lack of Tim44 recruitment led to an almost complete dissociation of Tim14-Tim16 pair from the Tim17-Tim23 core.
source: Lack of Tim44 recruitment also led to an almost complete dissociation of Tim14-Tim16 pair from the Tim17-Tim23 core, supporting the previous finding that Tim44 is the major component that connects the Tim17-Tim23 with the Tim14-Tim16 subcomplex (Kozany et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation and supported by a citation.

claim: Tim44 is the major component that connects the Tim17-Tim23 with the Tim14-Tim16 subcomplex.
source: Lack of Tim44 recruitment also led to an almost complete dissociation of Tim14-Tim16 pair from the Tim17-Tim23 core, supporting the previous finding that Tim44 is the major component that connects the Tim17-Tim23 with the Tim14-Tim16 subcomplex (Kozany et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and confirmed by the current data.

claim: Lack of coprecipitation of Tim44 with Tim23 antibodies from lysates of the R105A mutant mitochondria supports the notion that Tim17 is the major component for recruitment of Tim44 to the Tim17-Tim23 core.
source: Lack of coprecipitation of Tim44 with Tim23 antibodies from lysates of the R105A mutant mitochondria further supports the notion that Tim17 is the major component for recruitment of Tim44 to the Tim17-Tim23 core (Banerjee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: Tim17 is the major component for recruitment of Tim44 to the Tim17-Tim23 core.
source: Lack of coprecipitation of Tim44 with Tim23 antibodies from lysates of the R105A mutant mitochondria further supports the notion that Tim17 is the major component for recruitment of Tim44 to the Tim17-Tim23 core (Banerjee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: Essentially the same observations were made when Tim17R105K mutant mitochondria were analyzed by coimmunoprecipitation.
source: Essentially the same observations were made when Tim17R105K mutant mitochondria were analyzed by coimmunoprecipitation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), again suggesting that it is not the positive charge per se that is functionally and/or structurally important.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: It is not the positive charge per se at position 105 that is functionally and/or structurally important.
source: Essentially the same observations were made when Tim17R105K mutant mitochondria were analyzed by coimmunoprecipitation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), again suggesting that it is not the positive charge per se that is functionally and/or structurally important.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that R105K behaves similarly to R105A.

claim: When BPA was introduced at position 106 of Tim17, an additional band was observed upon immunoblotting with Tim44 antibodies.
source: When BPA was introduced at position 106 of Tim17, an additional band was observed upon immunoblotting with Tim44 antibodies (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The crosslinked band between Tim17(106BPA) and Tim44 was present only in UV-treated cells.
source: This band was present only in UV-treated cells demonstrating the specificity of the crosslink.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from crosslinking experiments.

claim: The crosslinked species between Tim17(106BPA) and Tim44 was efficiently recovered in the bound fraction of Ni-agarose beads.
source: The crosslinked species was efficiently recovered in the bound fraction, in contrast to the non-crosslinked Tim44.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The crosslinked band represents a crosslink between Tim17 and Tim44.
source: Since this band was recognized by Tim44 antibodies and it bound to Ni-agarose beads, we conclude that it represents a crosslink between Tim17 and Tim44.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations from crosslinking and pull-down experiments.

claim: In Tim17 containing both the R105A mutation and BPA at position 106, no crosslink between Tim17 and Tim44 was observed.
source: In the end, we made a version of Tim17 containing both the R105A mutation and BPA introduced at position 106. In this mutant, no crosslink between Tim17 and Tim44 was observed (Figure 3E), providing further support for the involvement of R105 in Tim44 binding.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The absence of crosslink in R105A/106BPA provides further support for the involvement of R105 in Tim44 binding.
source: In the end, we made a version of Tim17 containing both the R105A mutation and BPA introduced at position 106. In this mutant, no crosslink between Tim17 and Tim44 was observed (Figure 3E), providing further support for the involvement of R105 in Tim44 binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation.

claim: The TMs of Tim17 have functionally distinct roles.
source: Here, we have functionally dissected the TM segments of Tim17. Our data show that the TMs of Tim17 have functionally distinct roles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In Tim17, unlike in Tim23, TMs 1 and 2 are not sufficient to support the function of the full length protein.
source: This notion is further supported by the observation that in Tim17, unlike in Tim23 (Pareek et al., 2013), TMs 1 and 2 are not sufficient to support the function of the full length protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and comparison with cited previous work.

claim: TMs 1 and 2 of Tim17 are involved, directly or indirectly, in the interaction with Tim23.
source: Our data support a model in which TMs 1 and 2 are involved, directly or indirectly, in the interaction with Tim23 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The first two TMs in the members of the Tim17/Tim23 protein family are involved in formation of higher order structures.
source: Although the exact arrangement of the TMs remains currently unknown, the available data suggest that the first two TMs in the members of this protein family are involved in formation of higher order structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from this study and previous work.

claim: A recently identified disulfide bond in Tim17 appears to play a role in formation of higher order structures.
source: A recently identified disulfide bond in Tim17 appears to play a role in this process (Mokranjac, 2016; Ramesh et al., 2016; Wrobel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The second half of Tim17, and in particular a strictly conserved arginine residue at the matrix-facing side of IM, play an essential role in recruitment of Tim44.
source: In addition, we found that the second half of Tim17, and in particular a strictly conserved arginine residue at the matrix-facing side of IM, play an essential role in recruitment of Tim44 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tim17 may bridge the translocation channel and the import motor of the TIM23 complex.
source: Thus, Tim17 may bridge the translocation channel and the import motor of the TIM23 complex suggesting how the translocating proteins are guided between the two.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Tim17 may be involved in guiding translocating proteins from the channel to the import motor.
source: Thus, Tim17 may bridge the translocation channel and the import motor of the TIM23 complex suggesting how the translocating proteins are guided between the two.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Deletion of TIM17 is lethal.
source: Since deletion of TIM17 is lethal, mutants were introduced into a Tim17 shuffling strain, a TIM17 deletion strain rescued by a wild type (wt) copy of the protein encoded on a URA plasmid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tim17 essentiality.

claim: All experiments shown are typical representatives of experiments performed at least three times.
source: All the experiments shown are typical representatives of experiments performed at least three times.
evidence: This is a statement about the reproducibility of the experimental data.

claim: All critical experiments were performed with at least three biological replicates.
source: To ensure reproducibility, all the critical experiments were not only performed with at least three biological replicates but were also repeated by at least two researchers, in some cases even in two different laboratories.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methodology and reproducibility.

source: To ensure reproducibility, all the critical experiments were not only performed with at least three biological replicates but were also repeated by at least two researchers, in some cases even in two different laboratories.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methodology and reproducibility.
